College radio submissions for independent artists

By the RadioReach team Updated August 18, 2026 3 min read Core guides

On this page
  • Who should you contact at a college radio station?
  • How should you submit music to college radio?
  • When should you submit?
  • Do college radio stations accept independent music?
  • Charts, adds, and spins: what happens after you submit
  • Where a radio contact list helps

College radio remains one of the most approachable parts of the radio ecosystem for independent musicians, but the process is rarely as simple as sending the same email to every station. Different stations have different formats, schedules, submission rules, and decision-makers. A useful campaign starts by identifying stations that actually make sense for your music — then respecting how each one wants to be contacted.

Who should you contact at a college radio station?

Look first for a music director, genre director, program director, specialty-show host, or a clearly identified music-submission address. A general station inbox can still be useful when no individual contact is published, but a relevant human contact is usually better than sending blindly.

Titles vary from station to station. Some student-run stations divide responsibility by genre — a hip-hop director, a loud-rock director, an electronic director. Others have one music director handling most incoming releases. Read the station's own website before assuming who makes programming decisions.

How should you submit music to college radio?

Follow the station's stated submission process first. If it accepts digital submissions, send a concise message identifying the artist, genre, release, relevant location or story, and a streaming link. Avoid enormous attachments unless the station specifically asks for them — a private streaming link or a download page is the standard.

The strongest outreach usually explains why the release belongs at that particular station. Mentioning a relevant specialty show, a regional connection, or an obvious programming fit is more useful than claiming that a track is simply "perfect for radio."

When should you submit?

College stations run on academic calendars, and staffing changes every semester. Two rhythms matter:

  • Semester turnover: a music director who loved your genre may graduate in May. Contact lists go stale fast, so verify you are writing to the current decision-maker each campaign.
  • Seasonal timing: the fall (roughly September–November) and spring (February–April) semesters are when full staffs are active and charts are busy. Summer often means skeleton crews and slower responses — not a rejection.

For a new release, aim to pitch two to four weeks before your release date. If the song is already out, pitch it anyway — many stations add music that is a few months old, especially for specialty shows.

Do college radio stations accept independent music?

Many do, although policies vary widely. College and noncommercial stations often have more programming flexibility than large commercial stations, and specialty programs may actively seek music outside major-label pipelines. That does not mean every station accepts unsolicited music, or that a submission guarantees airplay.

Treat the station's published rules as authoritative. Radio promotion works better as targeted research than as mass email — one well-matched station is worth more than fifty that will never play you.

Charts, adds, and spins: what happens after you submit

If a music director adds your track, airplay may show up in the station's playlist logs and — at stations that report to the NACC charts — in weekly genre chart tallies. An add means the station has put your song into rotation; spins are the individual plays that follow.

You will not see most of this happen. Stations rarely announce adds, so build a simple tracking habit: check station playlists and charts weekly for your artist name, and log whatever you find. A handful of confirmed spins is real, quotable momentum you can mention in your next round of pitches.

Frequently asked questions

How far in advance should I submit to college radio?

Most music directors prefer to receive music two to four weeks before your release date, while the track is still new to them but easy to schedule. If you care about chart reporting, submitting slightly before release gives a station time to add it the week the song goes public.

Do college radio stations only play label-submitted music?

No. College and community stations are among the most open parts of the radio ecosystem to direct artist submissions. Many actively prefer hearing from independent artists, as long as the pitch fits the station's programming and follows its stated process.

Should I send a physical CD or vinyl?

Default to digital unless the station or show says otherwise. Some specialty shows and DJs still enjoy physical copies, but an unsolicited package costs you money and usually lands in a pile. Check the station's submission page — when a physical copy is welcome, it will say so.

How many times should I follow up?

Once. If a music director has not replied seven to ten days after your initial pitch, send one short, polite nudge with the original details below it. After that, assume the answer is not yet and move your energy to the next station.

What is NACC and why do artists mention it?

The North American College and Community Radio (NACC) charts aggregate airplay reported by hundreds of college and community stations in the US and Canada. Getting added at reporting stations can place your release on genre charts that programmers watch. Our glossary covers NACC and other chart terms in more depth.
